name: Warrenpoint
title: Warrenpoint Hull Gauging: UTM on Carlingford Lough
description: Thickness measurement at Warrenpoint Harbour, Carlingford Lough: ro-ro freight ships on the Heysham route, bulk carriers and coasters, holds, tanks and decks.
h1: Ultrasonic Thickness Measurement for Ships at Warrenpoint Harbour
intro: Warrenpoint Harbour stands near the head of Carlingford Lough in County Down and is the second-largest port in Northern Ireland. Its high-frequency ro-ro freight link to Heysham, now run by CLdN under a long-term agreement with the harbour, is the core of the business, and bulk carriers, coasters and general cargo ships bring grain, animal feed and timber. Freight ships returning on a fixed schedule suit staged gauging, while bulk calls give days alongside. Every job is carried out by technicians who travel from India to the vessel.
keywords: bulk carrier hold gauging county down

highlights.h: A ro-ro route on a fixed schedule
highlights.p: The Heysham freight ships come back to the same berth on a regular cycle, so trailer-deck, ramp and ballast tank readings can be split over several calls without disturbing the timetable. The operator and terminal know the sailing times well in advance, which makes each visit easy to plan.

highlights.h: Bulk discharges with time to work
highlights.p: Grain and feed carriers discharging at the deep-water quay commonly stay for more than one tide. Holds can be gauged as they empty, and topside and hopper tanks opened when the crew can ventilate them, so one call can give a full hold-and-tank picture.

highlights.h: A lough shared with the Republic
highlights.p: Carlingford Lough has Warrenpoint near its head on the northern side and the Irish port of Greenore on the southern shore near the entrance. Ships for both use the same approach channel, but which regulator a ship deals with depends on the shore it berths at.

port.h: Warrenpoint: a trust port near the head of Carlingford Lough
p: Carlingford Lough is a glacial sea inlet running between the Mourne Mountains on the County Down side and the Cooley peninsula in County Louth, and Warrenpoint lies close to its inner end, where the Newry River comes in. Ships enter from the Irish Sea past the rocks at the lough mouth, marked by the Haulbowline lighthouse, and follow a buoyed channel up the lough to the harbour. The passage is tidal and ships normally take a pilot, so arrivals are planned to the tide and the berthing time is usually known well before the ship crosses the entrance. Inside, high ground on both shores gives good shelter from most directions, although the lough can funnel strong winds along its length. Newry and its canal lie further inland, but today's commercial shipping stops at Warrenpoint.

Warrenpoint Harbour Authority became a trust port by legislation in 1971, and the harbour has grown steadily since, adding a deep-water quay, new ro-ro berthing and covered storage. Its largest customer is the freight service to Heysham in Lancashire, built up by Seatruck and now operated by CLdN, which signed a 55-year operating agreement with the harbour that took effect at the start of 2026. The route carries trailers and trade cars between Northern Ireland and Great Britain, from quarrying machinery built in Mid Ulster to aerospace components and food products. Alongside it, bulk carriers and coasters bring grain, animal feed and other agricultural cargoes for the farms of Down, Armagh and the border counties, and timber and forest products arrive for the building trade, with general and break-bulk cargo making up the rest.

Two kinds of inspection time are on offer here. The ro-ro ships keep to a timetable and spend a fairly short spell at the berth on each call, but they return so often that a scope worth several days on board can be divided into instalments. Bulk ships and coasters arrive less predictably, yet a discharge of grain or timber can take a day or more, during which holds and tanks can be opened in turn. Coasters on regular feed and fertiliser runs often reappear every few weeks, letting a condition programme run over months for an owner who wants to watch wastage develop. The harbour has no drydock, so dockings are arranged away from the lough, and readings taken at Warrenpoint are usually the groundwork for that docking or for an owner deciding whether a ship is worth keeping in service.

facilities.h: Where gauging is done at Warrenpoint
p: The ro-ro berths are the busiest part of the harbour. On a Heysham freight ship, the team works with the terminal and the chief officer, taking trailer-deck plating, ramp structure and lashing points in lanes that are clear, then moving into ballast tanks and void spaces the crew prepared before arrival. These ships carry drivers rather than a full passenger complement, and their loading pattern is simpler than a ro-pax ferry's, so releasing deck areas is often more flexible, although the turnaround remains the controlling factor on every call.

The deep-water quay and the general cargo berths take bulk carriers, coasters and break-bulk ships, and that is where most hold and tank gauging takes place. Grain and feed residues must be removed before plate readings are worth taking, so cleaning is written into the plan with the stevedores and the crew. For work that needs dry access to the outside of the hull, a ship trading to Warrenpoint docks elsewhere, usually at Belfast, on the Mersey or in a continental yard. If a ship has to wait outside the lough for the tide, launch boarding is possible through the agent, but the water there is open and the window short.
list: Ro-ro freight berths — trailer-deck, ramp and ballast tank readings on Heysham-route ships, staged across calls.
Deep-water quay — hold, hopper and topside tank gauging on grain and feed carriers during discharge.
General cargo berths — hatch cover, coaming and deck gauging on timber and break-bulk ships.
Coasters on regular trades — small tank and piping scopes repeated over several visits by the same ship.
Dockings elsewhere — internal structure gauged at Warrenpoint before a drydock at Belfast or a yard in Britain.

context.h: Rules and regulators for ships calling at Warrenpoint
p: Warrenpoint is in the UK, so the Maritime and Coastguard Agency carries out port state control there under the Paris MoU, while Greenore on the opposite shore of the same lough falls to Ireland's Marine Survey Office. Two inspection authorities on one stretch of water is unusual, and it occasionally matters to a master whose ship calls at both ports on a single trip. For the bulk and general cargo ships that make up most of the traffic outside the ro-ro trade, many of them older tonnage, PSC attention tends to settle on hatch covers, hold structure, ballast tanks and the condition of air pipes and vents on deck, all of which can be measured while the cargo comes out.

Sailings between Warrenpoint and Heysham connect two UK ports and therefore sit outside the EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime, whereas a ship arriving from an Irish or continental port carries EU obligations for that leg. The length of the CLdN agreement points to a route that will be served for decades, and keeping freight ships on it over a long working life depends on knowing how their decks, ramps and tanks are wearing. Regular gauging between dockings gives the operator that record and lets refit steelwork be planned in advance instead of discovered once the ship is already in dock.

jobs.h: Typical thickness gauging jobs at Warrenpoint
jobs.p: At Warrenpoint we see two kinds of job. Freight ship work is planned with the operator and divided across calls, so a full pre-refit scope is gathered without holding a ship in port. Bulk and general cargo work is planned call by call, usually for an owner or manager who wants condition figures before a survey, a docking or a sale. Crack checks with MPI are often added on ramps and lashing points. In either case the scope is agreed in advance with the superintendent, and readings are reported in class TM formats with the frame and strake references that the yard and the attending surveyor will work from.
list: Pre-refit gauging on a Heysham-route ro-ro freight ship, staged over several weeks of calls.
Trailer-deck and ramp inspection after damage, with UT for wastage and MPI on hinge lugs.
Hold and ballast tank gauging on a grain carrier discharging at the deep-water quay, ahead of an intermediate survey.
Owner's condition gauging on a coaster in the feed trade before a decision on steel renewal or sale.
Hatch cover and coaming readings on a timber ship after water ingress was reported on passage.

logistics: Belfast International, George Best Belfast City and Dublin airports are the usual arrival points for a Warrenpoint job, with the harbour reached by road. Dublin is often convenient for long-haul flights, but a team landing there must also hold permission for the UK, because the job itself is in Northern Ireland. We secure UK visas once the dates are firm and, where the route needs it, Irish entry as well. Harbour access and berth passes are arranged through the ship's agent and the harbour authority.

faqs.q: Can a Heysham ro-ro ship be gauged during its turnaround?
faqs.a: Yes, in instalments. Each call is limited by the loading plan, so the team takes a section of trailer deck, a ramp or one or two prepared ballast tanks per visit and keeps the same reference points every time. Because the ship returns so often, a full scope can be collected over a few weeks without altering the timetable, and the consolidated report is ready before the refit.

faqs.q: How long does a bulk carrier stay alongside at Warrenpoint?
faqs.a: It depends on the cargo and the size of the ship, but grain, feed and timber discharges commonly take more than a day. That is usually enough for hold gauging behind the discharge and for opening some ballast tanks. We confirm the expected stay with the agent before mobilising and order the scope so that the items the superintendent needs most are measured first.

faqs.q: Do you also work at Greenore on the other side of the lough?
faqs.a: We can, but Greenore is a separate port in Ireland, with Irish port state control and Irish immigration rules for the team. A ship calling at both Warrenpoint and Greenore can be gauged at either, and we arrange the visas so that the team is covered for whichever port the work actually falls in, with access arranged through the agent at each.

faqs.q: Is there anywhere to dock a ship near Warrenpoint?
faqs.a: Not on Carlingford Lough. Ships trading here go to Belfast, the nearest drydock, or to yards in Britain or on the Continent. We often gauge internal structure and piping at Warrenpoint before such a docking, so the superintendent can send the yard a steel and pipe estimate and the docking can begin with material already on order.
